tei:titleStmt.tei:title: קְדוּשְׁתָּאוֹת לְשַׁבָּת הַגָּדוֹל
Qedushtaot cycle and "seder" azhara for Shabbat haGadol, by Rabbi Yosef Bonfils (and Yannai)

tei:div.tei:head: Qedushtaot cycle and "seder" azhara for Shabbat haGadol, by Rabbi Yosef Bonfils (and Yannai)

tei:lg.tei:l: Blessed are You,
o Cause, our God and God of our ancestors.
God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob.
The Deity,
great and mighty and awesome;
the almighty Deity,
who well repays kindness,
and possesses all,
and remembers the kindnesses of ancestors
and sends a redeemer to their descendants
for Their Name’s sake,
in love.
Sovereign, Help
and Rescue and Shield —
Reshut
By the counsel of sages and scholars,
and the study of knowledge-understanders,
let me open my mouth in song and cheer
to thank and praise the countenance of the Dweller on High.
Magen
As You, God stepped out to strike Egypt’s southland,
Breaking into their troop, their fortresses to disband,
Cittern and lyre as You redeemed Your people’s band,
Delivering them, sifting like semolina mixed by hand.
Exiling to the valley the horde of Bubastis,
Floundering on the ground, borne down and abscessed.
Glowing, the once-forsaken, blood-coated, oppressed,
Had strengthened in bathing and in washing refreshed.
In advance of the bitter yokedness’ removal,
Jumped salvation for those guarded like a pupil.
Kitting out with a crown of soul-refreshing approval,
Letting them know first of the sabbath’s behooval.

tei:l.tei:note: In most modern Ashkenazi practice, the catenae of verses inserted after the first three piyyutim are not recited.

tei:lg.tei:l: As it is written:
See that the Cause gave you the sabbath,
thus They are giving you on the sixth day two days’ bread;
each man stay where he is,
let no man go out from his place
on the seventh day. (Exodus 16:29)
And it is said:
And I washed you in water
and I removed the blood from upon you
and I rubbed you with oil. (Ezekiel 16:9)
And it is said:
For as the land puts out its sprouts,
and a garden germinates its seeds,
thus the Master Cause
will germinate justice and praise
before all the nations. (Isaiah 61:11)
And it is said:
You saved with Your right hand Your people,
the chilren of Jacob and Joseph,
forever. (Psalms 77:16)
Forever may I exalt the Ruler and Securer,
Navigating me to liberty from the house of the obscurer.
Occulting my head, for the remnant to ensure her,
Protector and shield, bypasser and abjurer.
Blessed are You, o Cause, shield of Abraham.
You are mighty forever, Master,
You bring life to the dead, greatly saving.
You turn the wind
and send down the rain.
You provide for life in kindness,
reviving the dead in great mercy,
lift the fallen,
heal the sick,
free the bound,
and keep faith with sleepers in the dust.
Who is like You, Master of Powerful Acts,
and who can be compared to You?
Sovereign, who brings death and life
and causes salvation to sprout.
And trusted are You to revive the dead —
Meḥaiyeh
Quarantined prisoners, when they went out free,
Quagmire-drowned ones raising a miraculous burgee,
Rest and refreshment You reinforced them by decree,
Ratified before the soul’s remedy.
Signification and meaning You at Marah did ordain,
So as to understand completely its law pure and plain,
To set its sanctity by remembring and keeping twain,
To express cheer in thanksgiving and hymnal refrain.
Upon Tanis You did judgments great,
Unfurling a tent never to vacate.
Vanished are the foul ones, in rage to subjugate,
Vertigo seized Edom and Canaan to agitate.
As it is written:
Thus the chiliarchs of Edom were panicked,
the chieftains of Moab seized by trembling,
stunned were all the inhabitants of Canaan. (Exodus 15:15)
And it is said:
And you, speak to the children of Israel to say:
yet My sabbaths you will keep,
for it is a sign between Me and you for all ages,
to know that I the Cause santify you. (Exodus 31:13)
And it is said:
If you hold back your foot on the sabbath,
from doing your desires on My holy day,
and call the sabbath a delight,
the Cause’s holiness honored,
and honor it over going your ways,
finding your desires,
and speaking matters... (Isaiah 58:13)
And it is said:
And be delighted upon the Cause,
and They will give you the desires of your heart. (Psalms 37:4)
Your heart with Your eyes to Your palace return,
Extruding rich oil for Your people to earn.
Your temple and altar establish in turn,
Zephyring revival that the sleepers may discern.
Blessed are You, o Cause, who revives the dead.
Meshalesh
Yea, my Savior and Glory, my Refuge and Haven,
Opposing my oppressors, rises up, throws a glaive in;
Shading me with Their wings – the Cause’s flag I wave in!
Exacting and requiting my judgment on the craven.
Fluorescing was Their lamb above my head,
By swift cloud They rode, from my abusers I sped;
Overturning the fort of those who torment and shred,
Nurturing me, to Their remote shelter me They led.
From Their holy abode They bandaged my wound
Into my mouth salvation’s springs the Master spooned.
Learning to rest, to the sabbath I was attuned,
So with my father Jacob’s inheritance I was festooned.
As it is written:
Thus you will be delighted upon the Cause,
and I will make you ride on the high places of earth,
and I will feed you your father Jacob’s inheritance,
for the mouth of the Cause has spoken. (Isaiah 58:14)
And it is said:
Six days you will do your labor,
and on the seventh day you will cease,
so that your ox and your donkey will rest
and your maid’s son and the stranger will be refreshed. (Exodus 23:13)
And it is said:
Six days will your labor be done,
and on the seventh day a sabbath of sabbaths,
holy to the Cause;
all who do work on the sabbath day
will die, die! (Exodus 31:15)
And it is said:
My God, my Rock in whom I trust,
my Shield, the Horn of my salvation,
my Refuge and Haven,
my Savior, saving me from violence. (II Samuel 22:3)
And it is said:
The Cause reigns forever;
your God, Zion, from generation to generation;
praise Yah! (Psalms 146:10)
And You are holy, enthroned on Israel’s praise. (Psalms 22:4)
El Na
Deity, please!
The pleasant vineyard, the dandled germination,
Was chewed up by the teeth of the wicked’s mastication.
And You were revealed to free her from the criminals’ location,
In a nine-hundred-million-strong aggregation,
And in merit of he who at ninety-nine You gave consideration,
She was enriched with ninety laden mules’ allocation.
You cleared out kings and nobles before her destination;
She sent out her captains who rose up for salvation.
For her portion she took seven of the seventy nations,
For a tithe is given to the daughters by designation.
She wandered forty years in the land of desolation;
Food fit for a king they would eat to satiation,
Granting Their holiness, and chanting ululation:
Ḥai v-Qayyam
Living and enduring,
awesome and exalted
and holy!
You descended to save Your folk,
That Your sweet path they would evoke.
Turning Your steps to the ruins at a stroke,
To wrathfully suppress the oppressors’ yoke.
On the destruction of the despoilers’ hordes
Their forces were finished with their lords,
And the time of love came towards;
salvation sprouted for the beloved wards.
Secret coming out in exaltation —
The sorrowful would leave in refreshing liberation!
Envoys rushed to the captive nation —
“Two twins of a deer,” per the quotation.
Preparing for the banquet of the king,
The palace chef encountered them, saying:
“He whosoever comes before the king
Must bring before him a gift of something!”
Standing at the Casluhite gate,
The sent out messengers did wait.
Overwhelmed were those who pluck mallow for their plate,
“No handful or trickle, ingrate!”
Nessie, with a haughty heart,
Mustered his legions to compart.
“One who brings gifts may start,
And those without shall lastly depart!”
Frained the python, deaf and mute,
“Who was asked for, and for whose suit?
So they responded, “Twisted from the root;
They will remove them in removal absolute!”
Arrogant, he perversely rebelled,
“What’s it to me that They yelled?
Me They did not appease with any geld;
like one leaning on the staff he held!”
Upon this, to his godlets he did gaze,
“Is it so — in Their hands power stays?”
Exhibited, they did appraise:
“Among carcasses nothing Them portrays!
Lunatic, prepare to lose hard!
What would a priest do in a graveyard!
By the words’ own safeguard
Will the Master of Wonders have regard!
Enrobed in righteousness, They have been girt
To give to this evil man just desert!”
Strange man, his path They did pervert,
To his head returning all he did exert.
Raining locust-swarms, hail, and ignitions
Onto the master magicians
Nosediving, in smooth snakes’ position,
Gasping for earth’s dust in contrition.
Deity, please,
forever are You adored
and forever are You sanctified
and forever and aye will You reign and be exalted,
the Deity,
sovereign, awesome, high and holy,
for You are the Sovereign,
Sovereign of sovereigns, whose sovereignty is eternal;
tell Their awesomenesses,
recount Their strength,
glorify Their forces,
sanctify Them, exalt Them,
cheer, song, and laudation,
mighty praises of Their glory.
Qiqlar
Going out in speed,
You provided feed,
for satiety, not need;
holy!
Ardor great the people showed
By not complaining at the time bestowed
Cries of “What will we eat” like cows that lowed.
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
“Desert-bound we’ll go three days,”
Earlier the leader had told them, the guide on the ways;
Feigning not a thing from their gaze.
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Great speed, they rushed sanctifying those They called;
How they trusted in the Feeder of all They installed;
Indeed, just as those who revere Them go not unrecalled.
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Keeping this, the Only One saw it as a trait of renown.
“Let Me repay the youthful affection and kindness You’ve shown.
Meander after Me in the desert, in the land unsown!” (Jeremiah 2:2)
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Nests of vipers, cobra and scorpion and snake,
Over them the holy passed, while the hot sun did bake;
Puerile and elderly, and much cattle in their wake.
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Quick-wittedly, the flocks had knowledge to gain,
Rising still were the pieces they took from the grain,
Shoulder-borne, tied up in their cloaks like a chain.
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Taking bits of dough, unleavened cakes they made,
Vigorously pressed on their heads; whereby fermenting be stayed,
Exsiccated by yonder sun, on zyme-free bread they buffeted!
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Sixty-one baked meals ahead of time they prepared,
Breaking off nuggets from which they ate, kept, and shared,
In the end, lofty bread soared down on which they fared.
Going out in speed, You provided feed, for satiety, not need;
holy!
Rahit
And thus... it was in the middle of the night. (Exodus 12:29)
Most wondrous miracles You did at night.
At first watch, this very night.
You made the righteous convert victorious night.
when it was divided for him at
And it was in the middle of the night.
You judged Gerar’s king in dream of night.
You frightened the Aramean in dark night.
Israel wrestled and withstood an angel at night.
And it was in the middle of the night.
The firstborn seed of Upper Egypt You crushed at midnight.
Not finding their wealth when they rose at night.
The attack of Ḥaróshet’s leader You swept by stars of night.
And it was in the middle of the night.
The blasphemer planned to wave the desired;
You dressed him in corpses at night.
Bel and his pedestal were bent in pitch night.
The delightful man was shown secret visions of night.
And it was in the middle of the night.
The drinker from holy vessels was killed by night.
The one saved from the lions’s den
explained the mares-of-night.
The Agagite kept hatred and wrote books by night.
And it was in the middle of the night.
You roused victory on him by disturbing sleep at night.
You will stomp the press for the “watchman, what of night?” (Isaiah 21:11)
Yelling like a guard, saying, “morning has come, and also night!” (Isaiah 21:12)
And it was in the middle of the night.
Bring close the day neither day nor night!
High One, show that Yours is both day and night!
Appoint guards for Your city all day and all night!
Illuminate like daylight the darkness of night!
And it was in the middle of the night.
Reshut
And thus — all leaven do not eat. (Exodus 12:20)
Anxiously I come to stand
Before the holy ark at my post, as planned
Getting close, to cheer and declare grand
By permission of the Deity bannered over myriads grand.
Exultation of my Acquirer, I should make heard;
While I focus on investigating Their lawful word,
Zealously I plan, to knowledge spurred;
By interpretation of the honored sages of the seated herd.
To enthrone the Upholder of existence,
Jettisoning upon Them my burdensome resistance,
Contritely before Them I will walk a distance,
Let me open in halakhic talk with consistence.
My mouth’s words are overflowing;
Now let me sanctify the Kind and Easygoing;
Sonorously renewing knowing,
By permission of the order, holiness showing.
Present before the Speaker Upright
Championing words of pure light,
Quickly, let me ask — I’ll be polite —
Rabbi and comrade, permit this rite!
Shore up my strength, Surveyor in heaven,
That You favor my little handful, my steaven,
To clarify without fault
the laws of removing leaven.
Seder
As the God of the spirits of all flesh
delivered a law to Their people,
warning them in written rebuke
to search for leaven on the evening of the fourteenth,
by the time that people are no longer found in the market.
Candlelight is best for searching —
one may not search by sunlight or moonlight or torchlight —
and one must bless “on the removal of leaven” per the law.
Guard it carefully until the next day,
then immediately nullify the remainder with speech.
One should say thus: “All leaven that I have in my dwelling

tei:l.tei:seg: that I have not seen or removed should be nullified, made like dust.”

tei:lg.tei:l: Delayedly if it is found,
one is not liable for “Let it not be seen nor found” as a sin.
One who wants, after his search, to eat leaven to satiety
must put away his leftovers in in hiddenness.
Even if he examined all the nooks of the house,
leaving four or five loaves,

tei:l.tei:seg: if he finds that one of them is missing

tei:lg.tei:l: he must search again because a weasel might have taken it.
While our rabbis taught in their chapters
that the nooks and crannies of a house,
upper and lower ones are not searched,
but the middle ones are liable.
Zealously they explained: the sloped-roof of a veranda or cupboard,
a cowshed, a straw-barn, coops,
and locked storerooms of wine and oil,
do not mandate the search for leaven.
Hole in the wall between two people,
both of them must check as far as they can reach and nullify the rest.
But if between a Jew and a gentile he must remove it.
Palemo exempts him, lest the gentile say “He is a sorcerer and a mage!”
Taught they: one who embarks or goes out in a caravan,
not intending to return before Pesaḥ,
if it is less than thirty days before, he is required to remove leaven;
before thirty days he is not required to remove it.
In the case of a Jew with whom leaven is deposited

tei:l.tei:seg: and the owner is not there to take it,

tei:lg.tei:l: he can keep it until the fourth hour, as long as it can be eaten;
after the fourth hour if he has not arrived it is sold to a non-Jew.
Catastrophe struck regarding leaven on the eve of Pesaḥ?
If a dog certainly cannot find it, it is as if it is removed,
according to the open-eyed fellows.
And how far can a dog search? Three handbreaths.
Learn what they taught: salt-houses and wax-houses are stipulated,
as are date- and wood-houses,
mandated to be checked;
but a courtyard is exempt on account of ravens.
Mid-Pesaḥ, if one finds leaven in his house,
he covers it with a vessel so it cannot be seen.
But if it is consecrated he does not need to cover it,
because people keep away from it.

tei:l.tei:seg: Now sieves and metal bars and a kettle

tei:lg.tei:l: in which hot leavened dishes are cooked must be boiled;
set a smaller one in a larger one;

tei:l.tei:seg: for a larger one, make a rim and boil within over fire.
Say knives were used for hot leaven at meals.

tei:lg.tei:l: If it is possible to get new ones this is best,
but if not, boil them in hot water,
and in one vessel they are cleansed;
wooden spoons are stirred in boiling water.

tei:l.tei:seg: Onward they discoursed: basins and glazed containers and ceramic,
even if they can be boiled well, using them is forbidden,
and even if they are spacious and one can say the air dominates, them,
even so, the prohibition stands.

tei:lg.tei:l: Pots of ceramic do not need to be broken,
but set them aside until after Pesaḥ.
And plates are permitted if water is poured from a pot over them,
while stoneware is permitted through hot-rinsing.

tei:l.tei:seg: China with which leaven is used every day

tei:lg.tei:l: is like the sourdough container itself, whose fermenting is pungent.

tei:l.tei:seg: But if it touches it, then is removed, and is not kept there,
it is appropriate to use it.

tei:lg.tei:l: Quite alright to smear it with wine or oil,
however take care not to knead with it for the first nights.

tei:l.tei:seg: Maids and slaves not yet immersed

tei:lg.tei:l: may not knead it, that is the law.
Remembering the binding, matzo is made thin,
and for their sake must be guarded from fermentation, as is appropriate.
And the deaf-mute and mentally-deficient and minor do not knead, lest they err;

tei:l.tei:seg: even if a knowledgeable Jew bakes it they may not do so.

tei:lg.tei:l: Shouted they: never knead at once
more than five-fourths of flour, so too with ḥallah partitioning.
That is eggs per the count of “ḥallah,”
as the ‘omer demonstrates.
And a woman may only knead with water that was left overnight.
The pure ones taught in the praiseworthy Mishnah:
water used by a professional baker is poured out because it always causes fermentation.
And we taught: it ought to be spilled in an inclined place, so that none come to harm by it.
Finished are the laws of removal and boiling!
Juicy red wine is preferable
for the commandment
to fulfill a person’s requirement,
but if not, conditum and cooked wine in its place.
One quarter, no less,
must be in each of these four cups —
the same for men and women alike.
And apportion to children roast-grain and nuts so that they ask.
Scrupulously, they said, must women keep
all matters of Pesaḥ without err,
although they do not keep a time-bound commandment,
for anyone subject to “Do not eat leaven” is subject to “Eat matzo.”
Explaining in beautiful language, they said:
matzo and wine require reclining,
the bitter herb does not,

tei:l.tei:seg: as it requires thorough mastication.

tei:lg.tei:l: Falling on the right side is not reclining,
and what’s more, the windpipe could precede the esophagus and cause danger.

tei:l.tei:seg: Lying supine is not acceptable.

tei:lg.tei:l: And a woman does not need to, but if she is important then she ought to.
Serenely a son reclines in his father’s presence;
a student should not be disrespectful before his teacher,
but a craftsman’s apprentice certainly must recline.
And a waiter who ate an olive’s bulk of matzo while reclining has fulfilled his obligation.
Advocated they: grab the matzo on the Pesaḥ nights
so that the blossoming flowers should not sleep.
And we are required on the pilgrimage to be happy —
in the Temple with meat, and nowadays with spiced wine.
Mandated are women to rejoice and cheer,
in Babylon with colorful clothing,
in the land of Israel with pressed white linen,
while men enjoy themselves with wine.
Upon the eve of Pesaḥ, from around the time of the first afternoon service,
one may not eat until the exact time.
And upon coming from the house of whispered prayers,
they pour him the first cup.
Entering with blessing over the wine,
after that the sanctification and the time-blessing, but he does not speak of miracles yet,
for it must be mentioned in the Haggadah and it is unbefitting to repeat it.
And he drinks and washes his hands and blesses “on the raising of hands.”

tei:l.tei:seg: Let him take arugula or celery or cilantro or lettuce,

tei:lg.tei:l: and dips it in the ḥaroset and says “Creator of the fruit of the earth,”
and when he has eaten, he splits one of the three matzot, without a corresponding blessing —
half on the plate and half he puts on the table.
Set from the plate two cooked dishes,

tei:l.tei:seg: such as meat and roast fish,
or alternatively roast and boiled,

tei:lg.tei:l: and raise the plate and say “This is the poor-bread” etc.
On this, pour him the second cup of these cups,
and here the son asks his father,
“What makes this night different from other nights?”
And the rest of the haggadah until “Redeemer of Israel.”
Now that he has drank, he washes his hands,
and blesses “on the raising of hands” alone,
and from start to finish says “Who brings forth” over the upper of the two whole ones,

tei:l.tei:seg: but does not eat from it just yet.

tei:lg.tei:l: Snapped pieces he takes and blesses “to eat matzo” in speech,
and alongside the one on which he said “Who brings forth” he eats both,
and blesses on the romaine “to eat bitter-herbs” and dips it lightly,
and returns and eats matzo and bitter-herbs without a blessing and makes a unified sandwich as Hillel did.

tei:l.tei:seg: Then he may go to other houses and do as such up to here.

tei:lg.tei:l: And after that they do their meal as they need,
and a final olive’s bulk of matzo at the end must be consumed,
then wash without a blessing, for post-eating water is required but does not reqire a blessing.
Remembering at the third cup his grace after meals —
though at other houses he does not drink from the grace-cup —
and with the forth, he repeats the Egyptian hallel,
eating nothing else at that specific time,
only he can drink water.
If he is sick or asthenic
and is forced that he must drink wine,
let him say girt with the fifth cup the great hallel.
Now the Pesaḥ order is finished per its practices,
per all its rulings and laws;
just as we merited to order it,
so too may we merit to do it!
God, pure, dwelling on high,
raise the community of the uncountable congregation.
Speedily lead Your planted stalks,
redeemed, to Zion in cheer!
Silluq
And thus, to You holiness ascends,
For You are the Holy One and Savior of Israel.
None can arrange before Your to speak or to tell
the magnitude of Your wondrous miracles to understand and to explain.
How glorious is Your kindness, You set firm man’s footsteps!
Exceedingly deep are Your thoughts; You grant might and strength to empower.
And humankind in Your shadow shelters, long of pinion;
You increased the nation and greatened the joy for the children of Eber.
When the wicked one ruled over the poor people awaiting Your salvation,
You girded Yourself with Your graciousness upon the scattered and dispersed people to gather and connect them,
and You aroused the love of those sleeping in Ḥebron, laying in the grave,
and judged monetary and corporal judgment upon the magician-fellows,
and crushed them with blood and frogs ande lice and mixture and pestilence,
and shattered the heads of the crocodile who meddled in a debate not his.
For before a fall comes pride, and arrogance before shattering.
How can the flower of the field, whose days are a passing shadow,
be brazen against the Highest of the highest who breaks and shatters mountains?
They are the Master of vengeance, the God of justice, speaking righteousness,
making salvation sprout for those hoping in Them, and subjecting peoples under them.
And upon us They did wondrous mercy and raised a banner,
and avenged our vengeance over all the masters of force,
and subjugated in rage and stress the youths of Heliopolis and Heracleopolis,
between the kneading of dough and its leavening judging them to penalize their virilities.
And the belt of Their loins They strengthened and fortified to gird,
They split the sea and made them pass through, They gathered the currents up like heaps,
and in an unsown land They sustained and provided for them;
thus it is upon us to give thanks for each and every miracle.
Why does the Pesaḥ-offering come from the flock?
For They passed over and spared those called “the flock,”
and like a shepherd gathering up lambs drew them out and redeemed them from the mocking masters.
And why was it taken four days before it was slaughtered,
and given to the circumcised but void from the uncircumcised at that time?
So that they would have found in their hands commandments that may be delighting,
for already the era of loving and the time of the oath has come,
and they were winnowing in two bloods so that salvation would sprout.
And why was its blood placed on the lintel and the two doorposts,
which are the three altars in visible places to be seen?
They are an allegorical memorial of the three altars that the father of multitudes built consecutively,
in Dan, Beth-el, and the terebinth of Moreh.
And why may we eat leaven until the sixth hour?
As a memorial of the Presence’s speed in making wicked decrees pass away —
leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.
And why do we eat matzo, the poor-bread?
Because the dough did not have enough time to ferment before they were redeemed from poverty.
And why with bitter-herbs, which start soft and end hard?
Because they were bittered at first with a soft mouth, and at the end with a hard yoke.
And why are they dipped in ḥaroset?
As a memorial of the mortar that husband and wife would tread.
And why are spices mixed into it, kneaded up like clay?
As a memorial of the people scattering to gather up stubble for straw.
And why are two kinds of meat are put beside the loaf?
One as a memorial of the Pesaḥ-offering, and one as a memorial of the festival-offering.
And why is the plate removed before its time?
So that the child will see and ask “What makes this different?”
And why do other vegetables come first?
To exempt the commanded romaine from the blessing befitting it.
and since we do not say two blessings on one beverage or food,
just as it is impossible to eat or drink when one has already filled his gut.
Thus two matzot exempt from loaf to loaf,
since we do not repeat with two blessings,
we bless on this one and on that one and do not eat until we have finished both blessings.
And why are four cups commanded for this night?
As a memorial for the four redemptions that were heralded to the treasured people —
bringing and rescuing and taking and redeeming —
and to thank with them and give with them praise
to the One who struck the four cups of the handsome heifer,
and to shatter the nations, the disgusting and foul peoples
with four cups as written for them which are the cup of wrath,
and corresponding to them to make us drink four cups of compassion.
And why do we recline on a gloriously decorated bed?
As a memorial of the freedom, and the massed clouds of glory in our enveloping.
For thus is the practice of princes to go about in glory and ostentation,
for Jacob’s Holy One crowned us with a crown of royalty and praise,
and clearly made known that Their pastured people will be Their inheritance-people,
for to God are the powers fo the world, greatly exalted. (Psalms 47:10)
Exalted in holiness is the Lofty and Holy,
for a holy God are They in all kinds of holiness;
Their way is in holiness
and Their practice is in holiness;
Their word is in holiness,
Their seat is in holiness,
Their outstretched arm is in holiness,
beautiful and mighty in holiness!
They are holy
and Their people is holy
and all Their camps are holy;
none is like Their holiness
and none is akin to Them!
Sanctified in those close to Them,
and awesome over all surrounding Them,
and terrific in the council of the holy,
awesome in the myriads of lion-angels,
and the holy divine-angels compose song and praise,
in the holy song of the holy watcher-angels,
thundering and sanctifying
in the holy of holies,
at times silent,
and at times speaking, and in mornings renewed,
surrounding the throne of the chariot and articulating the holiness of the Name,
and sanctifying the threefold holiness of the Holy and Awesome...

tei:note.tei:p: This brief reshut is inserted into the Ashkenazi rite here to justify the practice of inserting piyyutim.
In the Hebrew, Patros From the Egyptian pꜣ-tꜣ-rsj (the land of the south), this term referred to Upper Egypt, the area of the Nile Valley south of the delta.
In the Hebrew, Pi-beset. Find Ezekiel 30:17
The last word ‘selah’ was originally a musical instruction, but in rabbinic interpretation it refers to eternity.
In Hebrew, Tso’an. An important city in New-Kingdom Egypt, often used as a synechdoche for the entire nation.

Note that in most Ashkenazi practice today this word is read עֲמָלֵק “in Amaleq,” almost certainly a censorship on behalf of a church well aware of Jewish usage of “Edom” as a euphemism. The next verse in the catena mentions Edom directly, but, of course, in modern Ashkenazi practice the catenae are skipped so the censorship is less obvious.
Found in Parma 3136 but not Berlin 1224.
Berlin 1224 includes an additional “and it is said” halfway through this verse, and continues with Isaiah 58:14.This is likely a scribal error since the next catena begins with it.

In modern Ashkenazi practice, as the catenae are skipped, this word is vocalized with the non-pausa form לִבְּךָ, as would be expected if it were not a direct citation of the last word of Psalms 37:4.
Found in Parma 3136 but not Berlin 1224.

In Berlin 1224 it was intended by the scribe, who seems to have begun writing on autopilot and ends up with an imaginary verse: ...וביום השביעי שבתון מקרא קודש כל מלאכת עבודה לא תעשו. ...and on the seventh day, a Sabbath of sabbaths, a holy occasion, all laborious work you shall not do. This is not in the Bible, which uses מלאכת עבודה to refer to work forbidden on festivals, a smaller category than work forbidden on Shabbat.
Abraham, who had a son at 99

As in, literally a tenth. The people Israel legendarily defeated seven nations in the process of conquering the land. Based on the idea that there are a total of seventy nations, Israel defeated a tenth of them.
Moses and Aaron, referring to the midrash on Song of Songs 4:5

Based on a phrase from Job 30:4, this phrase has traditionally been treated as an allegorical description of court flunkeys. But mallow, or molokhiyya, is still a very popular green vegetable in Egypt, so it might be literal as well.
Literally, Rahav — the primeval sea monster. Referring to Pharaoh, or Egypt in general. Find Isaiah 30:7 and Psalms 87:4
Referring to a beggar, who would have no money to offer as a gift.
As a metaphor. God would not be found among idols the same way a priest would not be found among corpses.
To cover from the exodus to the sixteenth of Iyyar, when the manna began to fall

Note that unlike the rest of this cycle, this rahit was written by Yannai. It is one of two portions of the Shabbat haGadol liturgical cycle which have, in Ashkenazi practice, been appended to the end of the Seder night. This translation was originally published as part of my haggadah last year.
Abraham. Find Genesis 15 and the “covenant between the pieces.”
Referring to Daniel. Find Daniel 7 for his night vision, and Daniel 10 for his moniker “delightful man.”
Daniel again. The lion’s den is in Daniel 6. He interprets nightmares in chapter 2.
Another reshut, this one asking permission to insert the seder (which follows immediately afterward).

The seder, or azharah, is a poetic halakhic discourse on the laws of Pesaḥ. The first half, an alphabetical acrostic, discusses the laws of searching for and disposing of leaven. The second half, a name-acrostic, discusses the laws of the seder night itself. As a halakhic discourse, it features a lot of Aramaic terminology, marked here in red. Because the point of the seder is the context rather than the poetic form, the translation does not preserve the rhyme scheme. However, the acrostic is preserved in order to help with following along.
Many texts here read וְעוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים “and a star-worshipper,” a medieval censorship.
Many texts here read הָעוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים “the star-worshipper,” a medieval censorship.

Here the second section of the poem begins, on the process of kashering dishes. This section, unlike the last, cites multiple passages not from Tractate Pesaḥim — some from the laws of boiling gentile-purchased dishes, and some from the Gaonic literature.
The matzo dough. Here the poem transitions to its third section, on the process of preparing matzo.
Of a qav, leading to around 1.7 kg.

The gematria of the word “ḥallah” is 43. According to Midrash Tanḥuma, Koraḥ 12:1, as cited in Halakhot Gedolot 11:7, 43.2 eggs is the number of eggs that qualifies dough for the ḥallah partitioning.
The ‘omer is a tenth of an ephah, and an ephah is 3 seah, which is 18 qav, which is 72 log, which is 432 eggs. This means that the ‘omer is 43.2 eggs.
And thus, the first acrostic is concluded. The second half of the poem focuses on the Seder night itself.
Proverbs 23:31, where it is used in quiet a negative context, despite its positive use here.

Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 10:1:11 says that conditum fulfills the obligation for wine at the seder night. What’s conditum? A variety of spiced and sweetened white wine that was beloved in ancient Rome. The Apicius, one of the best preserved Roman-era cookbooks, has a recipe. The Tasting History Youtube channel provides a translation here, also including a thankfully scaled-down version in case you aren’t making enough for an entire villa. I tried making conditum last year and it was surprisingly good! A very nice after-dinner apertif! If you do it yourself, definitely use long pepper — it adds a slight fruitiness that regular black pepper doesn’t have. And get good wildflower honey, something local. I’m not sure what the bay leaves did — maybe spikenard would have added more. I think it might work as a vermouth substitute in a mixed drink. Here’s a picture.
Of a log, around 75 mL. Pesaḥim 108b:5
Pesaḥim 108a:10. The Rema, in his mapah on the Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 472:4, says that all women are important.
Found in Seder Rav Amram’s order of Pesaḥ, page 1 of the 1865 Warsaw printing.

Many texts read וְאֵינוֹ מְבָרֵךְ ”but does not bless” here, to reflect the modern Ashkenazi practice whereein no blessing is said on washing before karpas. Bonfils clearly did say a blessing there, as do most Sephardim to this day.
As listed in Seder Rav Amram’s order of Pesaḥ, page 11 of the 1865 Warsaw printing
Nowadays most communities dip the karpas in saltwater or vinegar. However, in many communities the traditional practice was to dip in ḥaroset.

The earliest source for yaḥatz that I can find is Seder Rav Amram’s order of Pesaḥ, page 11 of the 1865 Warsaw printing. That being said, it does not mandate that the pieces are set in separate locations.

This passage, the beginning of Maggid, is of uncertain origin. Guggenheimer suggests it is a descendant of something that was recited in the Temple itself. In any case, the modern form is also first found in Seder Rav Amram’s order of Pesaḥ, page 10 of the 1865 Warsaw printing.

i.e. upon finishing the poor-bread declaration. The classic Ashkenazi practice, also attested in Rav Saadia Gaon. Ephraim of Bonn states that since the second cup is the cup of salvation, it is inappropriate to have it on the table when discussing poverty.. Many Sephardim, following Rav Amram Gaon and Maimonides, pour the second cup before the declaration.

Mishnah Pesaḥim 10:4 is the earliest source for the Temple-era four questions. However, in a post-Temple era roasted meat is no longer consumed as a seder ritual (and in many communities it is specifically avoided), so the currently asked questions are different.

The concluding blessing of the maggid. Based on Debra Reed Blank’s interpretation of גָּאַל as a nomen agentis akin to סַלָּח or גַנָּב in her essay “The Curious Theological Grammar of Ga’al Yisrael,” in The Experience of Jewish Liturgy (2011). For those who reject said interpretation this could be translated as “who redeemed.”

As found in most of the earlier sources. Only since the Rambam has the modern form עַל אֲכִילָת מַצָּה “on the eating of matzo” become normalized. The same is true for “to eat bitter-herbs” in the same stanza, which in modern haggadot is עַל אֲכִילָת מָרוֹר “on the eating of bitter-herbs.”

Referring to the festival hallel, Psalms 113 to 118. “Completes” is apropos, since the first two psalms are recited at the end of maggid instead. The name is first found in an Aramaic form in Berakhot 56a:16, and used to distinguish it from the “great hallel” of Psalms 136 — see below.
While not in the Vilna edition as found on Sefaria, this concept of the fifth cup said along with the great hallel is found in many manuscripts for Pesaḥim 118a.

These last two stanzas, from “Now the Pesaḥ order” on, have later, in Ashkenazi practice, been taken and added to the end of the seder night itself. In that location, the phrase “just as we merited to order it, so too may we merit to do it” is interpreted as “just as we merited to do the seder, so too may we merit to do the sacrifice.” However, in context, at the end of Bonfils’ seder poem, it means something very different: “just as we merited to recite the seder poem, so too may we merit to do the seder!”
Some texts read וּלְסַפֵּר “and to tell”
The great-great-great-great-grandfather of Abraham, and possible origin of the name “Hebrew”
Find Psalms 74:13. The crocodile represents Pharaoh — see Ezekiel 29:3.

Two major cities in Egypt. In the Hebrew, these cities are called On and Ḥanes, ultimately from the the Egyptian jwnw and hnn-nswt. Note that the name On, for Heliopolis, is revocalized here (as well as in Ezekiel 30:15) as Awen, meaning “evil.”
i.e. the plague of the firstborn, which struck before the dough could rise.

The centerpiece of the silluq, the following passage goes through several aspects of the seder and gives interpretations and explanations, serving almost as answers to the notoriously unanswered four questions.

According to Targum Yonatan on Ezekiel 16:6, the twofold repetition of “Live in your blood” in that verse — also the source for the imagery of wallowing, and found in the Haggadah — refers to the blood of the Pesaḥ sacrifice and the circumcision.

Abraham (the father of multitudes) builds three altars in Genesis 12:7, 12:8, and 13:18. Note, though, that none of them are built in Dan — they are built at Shechem, Bethel, and Moreh. Dan, however, is mentioned later in Abraham’s story, in the battle of the nine kings, in Genesis 14:14.

Referring to romaine, which is, in the wild, a biennial plant. In the first year its leaves are sweet and tender, and in the second year it grows a flower and its leaves wither and become bitter and tough. Pesaḥim 39a:10.
A pun on the rare word ferekh (rigor) in the Exodus story, found first in Sotah 11b:1.
Pesaḥim 115b:9. In many practices, the plate is removed from the table entirely before the maggid.
Normally one would say “Creator of the fruit of the earth” over the bitter-herbs, so we eat the other greens earlier so that we can say only the blessing of bitter-herbs themselves on them.
As in, we say the blessing of “who brings forth” on one and the blessing on matzo itself on the other loaf.
The four verbs of action in Exodus 6:7. This and the following interpretations of the four cups are found in Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 10:1:7.
The four repetitions of “cup” in Genesis 40:11–13
This entire line, from “and to shatter” to here, is censored in many texts. In some “peoples” is replaced with ‘Amaleq.
In Jeremiah 23:15, Jeremiah 51:7, Psalms 75:9, and Psalms 11:6
Conjugated in the plural, as sometimes occurs due to the pluralis majestatis nature of the Hebrew word “God.”
